distr::Gh object¶

The object form of the Gh family: it carries the parameters, and offers the density, the distribution function, random draws, the cumulant generating function and the cumulants as methods, and a maximum-likelihood fit with standard errors.

Signature¶

distr::Gh(double lambda, double alpha, double beta, double location, double scale);
distr::Gh::Gh(<one Series for each parameter>);   // a different distribution at every point
pluss::Series distr::Gh::pdf(const pluss::Series& x) const;
pluss::Series distr::Gh::logpdf(const pluss::Series& x) const;
pluss::Series distr::Gh::cdf(const pluss::Series& x) const;
pluss::Series distr::Gh::logcdf(const pluss::Series& x) const;
pluss::Series distr::Gh::sample(std::initializer_list<std::int64_t> sizes, pluss::Config cfg = {}, std::uint64_t seed = 0) const;
pluss::Series distr::Gh::sample_like(const pluss::Series& like, std::uint64_t seed = 0) const;
pluss::Series distr::Gh::cgf(const pluss::Series& t) const;
pluss::Series distr::Gh::cumulant(std::int64_t order) const;
distr::GhFit distr::Gh::MLE(const pluss::Series& x) const;

What It Does¶

distr::Gh holds the parameters of the Gh distribution, so that they are written once and the same object is used for every evaluation. Its methods give the same numbers as the kind-based functions distr::pdf(dst::Gh, ...) and the others, on a whole Series at once.

  • pdf, logpdf, cdf and logcdf evaluate the density, the distribution function and their logarithms.

  • sample draws a Series of the given shape; sample_like draws one with the shape and dtype of an existing Series. The seed fixes the stream.

  • cgf(t) is the cumulant generating function log E[exp(t X)], and cumulant(order) the cumulant of that order (the first is the mean, the second the variance).

  • A constructor taking a Series for each parameter makes an object that stands for a different distribution at every point: the density at the i-th point uses the i-th value of every parameter.

  • MLE(x) fits the family to observed values by maximum likelihood and returns a GhFit with the estimates (fields lambda, alpha, beta, location, scale), their standard errors, 95% intervals and the log-likelihood.

The parameters of the family are described on the Gh page.

Parameters¶

double lambda, double alpha, double beta, double location, double scale

lambda, alpha, beta, location and scale, in that order.

const pluss::Series& x

The points at which to evaluate, a Series of any shape; the result has the same shape.

std::initializer_list<std::int64_t> sizes

The shape of the array of random draws, for example {n} or {rows, columns}.

pluss::Config cfg

The dtype and platform of the draws; the default is Float32 on the CPU, so request Float64 when precision matters.

std::uint64_t seed

The seed of the stream. The same seed always gives the same draws; a seed of 0 is a fixed default, not a random one.

const pluss::Series& like

A Series whose shape and dtype sample_like copies for the draws; its values are not used.

const pluss::Series& t

The points at which to evaluate the cumulant generating function.

std::int64_t order

The order of the cumulant: 1 is the mean, 2 the variance, 3 the third cumulant, and so on.

<one Series for each parameter>

Parameters given as Series (all of one length, or one element each to broadcast) make an object that is a different distribution at every point of x.

const pluss::Series& x (for MLE)

The observed values to fit, one-dimensional and inside the support of the family.

Returns¶

pdf, logpdf, cdf, logcdf and cgf return a Series of the shape of their argument; sample and sample_like return the drawn Series; cumulant returns a one-element Series. MLE returns a GhFit.

Errors¶

  • Parameters outside their valid range are refused when a method is called (alpha must exceed abs(beta) and delta must be positive).

Methods¶

  • pdf – the density (mass function) at each point.

  • logpdf – the logarithm of the density.

  • cdf – the distribution function.

  • logcdf – the logarithm of the distribution function.

  • sample – random draws of a given shape.

  • sample_like – random draws with the shape and dtype of an existing Series.

  • cgf – the cumulant generating function.

  • cumulant – the cumulant of a given order.

  • MLE – the maximum-likelihood fit with standard errors and intervals.

Practical Examples¶

Example 1¶

Example 1 uses the object form, distr::Gh, which carries the parameters and offers the same functions as methods, plus cumulant for the moments.

#include <pluss/ma.h>

#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

namespace distr = pluss::subsp::stats::distr;
namespace dst = distr::dst;

int main() {
  const auto f64 = pluss::Config{}.with_dtype(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(5);

  const distr::Gh d{1.0, 1.5, -0.4, 0.1, 0.8};
  const auto sample = d.sample({200000}, f64, 11ULL);
  const auto at = pluss::make_series({1.0}, f64);

  std::cout << "pdf at 1: " << as_f64(d.pdf(at)) << '\n';
  std::cout << "cdf at 1: " << as_f64(d.cdf(at)) << '\n';
  const double m = as_f64(sample.mean());
  const double v = as_f64(((sample - m) * (sample - m)).mean());
  std::cout << "cumulant(1), the mean: " << as_f64(d.cumulant(1)) << "   mean of 200000 draws: " << m << '\n';
  std::cout << "cumulant(2), the variance: " << as_f64(d.cumulant(2)) << "   variance of the draws: " << v << '\n';
}

Output

pdf at 1: 0.14832
cdf at 1: 0.91172
cumulant(1), the mean: -0.44354   mean of 200000 draws: -0.44260
cumulant(2), the variance: 1.52852   variance of the draws: 1.52120

cumulant(1) and cumulant(2) are the exact mean (-0.44354) and variance (1.52852) of the distribution, computed from the parameters without drawing anything; the mean (-0.4426) and variance (1.5212) of 200000 draws land within sampling error of them (the standard error of the mean is about 0.00276).

Example 2¶

Example 2 uses every evaluation method of the object distr::Gh: the density (mass function), its logarithm, the distribution function and its logarithm, the cumulant generating function cgf, and the cumulants of orders 1 to 4.

#include <pluss/ma.h>

#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

namespace distr = pluss::subsp::stats::distr;
namespace dst = distr::dst;

int main() {
  const auto f64 = pluss::Config{}.with_dtype(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(5);

  const distr::Gh d{1.0, 1.5, -0.4, 0.1, 0.8};
  const auto x = pluss::make_series({-5.0, -2.0, 0.0, 1.0}, f64);
  const auto t = pluss::make_series({0.1, 0.2, 0.3}, f64);

  std::cout << "x:";
  for (double v : x.pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << "pdf:";
  for (double v : d.pdf(x).pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << "logpdf:";
  for (double v : d.logpdf(x).pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << "cdf:";
  for (double v : d.cdf(x).pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << "logcdf:";
  for (double v : d.logcdf(x).pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << "cgf at t = 0.1 0.2 0.3:";
  for (double v : d.cgf(t).pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';

  std::cout << "cumulants 1 to 4:";
  for (int order = 1; order <= 4; ++order) std::cout << ' ' << as_f64(d.cumulant(order));
  std::cout << '\n';
}

Output

x: -5.00000 -2.00000 0.00000 1.00000
pdf: 0.00431 0.10301 0.40193 0.14832
logpdf: -5.44567 -2.27296 -0.91147 -1.90837
cdf: 0.00397 0.09891 0.62711 0.91172
logcdf: -5.52838 -2.31357 -0.46663 -0.09242
cgf at t = 0.1 0.2 0.3: -0.03692 -0.05969 -0.06906
cumulants 1 to 4: -0.44354 1.52852 -1.39597 5.17185

logpdf and logcdf are the logarithms of the density and of the distribution function, computed directly, which is more accurate in the tails than taking the logarithm of a tiny number: at the first point exp(-5.44567) = 0.00431, the density 0.00431 printed above. The cumulants are -0.44354, 1.52852, -1.39597, 5.17185: the first is the mean, the second the variance, the third measures skewness (it is zero for a symmetric distribution), and the fourth the excess of the tails over a normal one. The cumulants are the Taylor coefficients of cgf: 0.1 κ1 + 0.1² κ2 / 2 + 0.1³ κ3 / 6 + 0.1⁴ κ4 / 24 = -0.03692 against cgf(0.1) = -0.03692.

Example 3¶

Example 3 draws random values from the object: sample_like takes the shape and dtype of an existing Series, sample takes a shape, and the seed fixes the stream; a large sample reproduces the first two cumulants.

#include <pluss/ma.h>

#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

namespace distr = pluss::subsp::stats::distr;
namespace dst = distr::dst;

int main() {
  const auto f64 = pluss::Config{}.with_dtype(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(5);

  const distr::Gh d{1.0, 1.5, -0.4, 0.1, 0.8};

  // sample_like draws a Series with the shape and dtype of an existing one; the seed fixes the stream.
  const auto like = pluss::series::zeros({2, 3}, f64);
  const auto draws = d.sample_like(like, 11ULL);
  std::cout << "shape of the draws: " << draws.sizes()[0] << " x " << draws.sizes()[1] << "\n";

  const auto again = d.sample_like(like, 11ULL);
  std::cout << "same seed, same draws: " << (as_f64((draws - again).abs().max()) == 0.0 ? "yes" : "no") << "\n";
  const auto other = d.sample_like(like, 12ULL);
  std::cout << "other seed, other draws: " << (as_f64((draws - other).abs().max()) > 0.0 ? "yes" : "no") << "\n";

  // sample takes the shape directly; a large sample estimates the mean and the variance.
  const auto big = d.sample({200000}, f64, 5ULL);
  const double m = as_f64(big.mean());
  const double v = as_f64(((big - m) * (big - m)).mean());
  std::cout << "mean of 200000 draws " << m << " (cumulant(1) = " << as_f64(d.cumulant(1)) << ")\n";
  std::cout << "variance of 200000 draws " << v << " (cumulant(2) = " << as_f64(d.cumulant(2)) << ")\n";
}

Output

shape of the draws: 2 x 3
same seed, same draws: yes
other seed, other draws: yes
mean of 200000 draws -0.44531 (cumulant(1) = -0.44354)
variance of 200000 draws 1.52315 (cumulant(2) = 1.52852)

Example 4¶

Example 4 gives the object a Series for each parameter. One object then stands for a different distribution at every point of x, and its density agrees with scalar objects built one point at a time.

#include <pluss/ma.h>

#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

namespace distr = pluss::subsp::stats::distr;
namespace dst = distr::dst;

int main() {
  const auto f64 = pluss::Config{}.with_dtype(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(5);

  // A Series for every parameter makes ONE object that is a different distribution at each point:
  // the density at the i-th point uses the i-th value of every parameter.
  const auto p0 = pluss::make_series({1.0, 1.25, 1.5}, f64);
  const auto p1 = pluss::make_series({1.5, 1.875, 2.25}, f64);
  const auto p2 = pluss::make_series({-0.4, -0.15000000000000002, 0.09999999999999998}, f64);
  const auto p3 = pluss::make_series({0.1, 0.35, 0.6}, f64);
  const auto p4 = pluss::make_series({0.8, 1.05, 1.3}, f64);
  const distr::Gh many{p0, p1, p2, p3, p4};
  const auto x = pluss::make_series({-5.0, -2.0, 0.0}, f64);
  const auto density = many.pdf(x);
  std::cout << "one object, three parameter sets:";
  for (double v : density.pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';

  // The same numbers, one scalar object at a time.
  {
    {
      const distr::Gh one{1.0, 1.5, -0.4, 0.1, 0.8};
      const auto at = pluss::make_series({-5.0}, f64);
      std::cout << "point 0: " << as_f64(density.select(0, 0)) << " and one object at a time " << as_f64(one.pdf(at)) << "\n";
    }
    {
      const distr::Gh one{1.25, 1.875, -0.15000000000000002, 0.35, 1.05};
      const auto at = pluss::make_series({-2.0}, f64);
      std::cout << "point 1: " << as_f64(density.select(0, 1)) << " and one object at a time " << as_f64(one.pdf(at)) << "\n";
    }
    {
      const distr::Gh one{1.5, 2.25, 0.09999999999999998, 0.6, 1.3};
      const auto at = pluss::make_series({0.0}, f64);
      std::cout << "point 2: " << as_f64(density.select(0, 2)) << " and one object at a time " << as_f64(one.pdf(at)) << "\n";
    }
  }
}

Output

one object, three parameter sets: 0.00431 0.04226 0.31659
point 0: 0.00431 and one object at a time 0.00431
point 1: 0.04226 and one object at a time 0.04226
point 2: 0.31659 and one object at a time 0.31659

One object with three values of each parameter returned the three densities 0.00431, 0.04226, 0.31659. Each equals the density of the scalar object built from the i-th values of the parameters and evaluated at the i-th point (the three lines below the first), so a Series-valued object is the same as three scalar objects without the loop.
